title: India Win Record Five Bronze Medals in Best-Ever Para Table Tennis Showing
excerpt: Bhavina Patel, Sonalben Patel, Prachi Pandey, Baby Sahana Ravi and Jehan Dorab Madan all reached the podium in singles at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Para Games.
body:
• India won five bronze medals in para table tennis singles at the Aichi-Nagoya 2026 Asian Para Games, beating the country's previous best of two bronze medals in the sport at the Games.
  • The medallists were Bhavina Patel (Class 4-5), Sonalben Patel (Class 3), Prachi Pandey (Class 6), Baby Sahana Ravi (Class 9) and Jehan Dorab Madan (men's Class 1), all after semifinal defeats.
  • Prachi Pandey and Baby Sahana Ravi became the first Indians to reach the para table tennis podium in the standing categories at the Asian Para Games.
  • For readers following the Games, all five medals came in singles, so India's para table tennis campaign in Aichi-Nagoya is already its strongest on record even before any further events are decided.

India recorded its best-ever para table tennis result at the Asian Para Games on Tuesday, winning five bronze medals in singles at the Aichi-Nagoya 2026 Games in Japan. Bhavina Patel, Sonalben Patel, Prachi Pandey and Baby Sahana Ravi won bronze in the women's singles, and Jehan Dorab Madan added a fifth bronze in the men's singles.

All five players lost in the semifinals, which in this format left them with bronze. The haul passed India's tally from the previous edition, where the country had won two bronze medals in para table tennis, according to The Bridge. It also came against experienced opposition: the report said the four women all went down to accomplished Paralympic medallists in their semifinals.

Bhavina Patel, a former Paralympic silver medallist, was beaten 7-11, 5-11, 7-11 by China's Zhang Bian in the Class 4-5 semifinal, MyKhel reported. Zhang is an eight-time Paralympic gold medallist. For Bhavina, 39 and from Gujarat, this was a second successive bronze at the Asian Para Games. She had won silver at the 2018 edition and gold at the 2022 Commonwealth Games, and at the Tokyo Paralympics she became the first Indian table tennis player to win a Paralympic medal.

Sonalben Patel lost by the same margin in games in Class 3, falling 7-11, 5-11, 6-11 to South Korea's Jiyu Yoon. Yoon is the defending champion and a three-time Paralympic medallist. Sonalben had previously won a doubles silver at the 2018 Jakarta Games. Class 3 is a wheelchair category for athletes with poor sitting balance and limited trunk control but normal or near-normal arm and hand function, while Class 4-5 is for wheelchair athletes who have full upper body control.

The two standing-category medals carried a separate first. Prachi Pandey went down 9-11, 2-11, 8-11 to reigning Paralympic champion Najlah Al-Dayyeni of Iraq in the Class 6 semifinal. Baby Sahana Ravi, from Tamil Nadu, lost 8-11, 2-11, 4-11 to five-time Paralympic gold medallist Mao Jingdian of China in Class 9. Together, Prachi and Sahana became India's first para table tennis players to make the podium in the standing categories at the Asian Para Games, as RevSportz and The Bridge both reported. Class 6 covers athletes with severe impairments in both arms and legs, and Class 9 covers athletes with mild physical impairments affecting their legs or playing arm, or severe impairments of the non-playing arm.

Jehan Dorab Madan completed the five in the men's singles Class 1, losing 3-0, by 11-4, 11-7, 11-3, to Kim Hyeonuk in his semifinal. Madan is a former racing driver from Chennai. A road accident in 2007, while he was on a business trip to Mumbai, left him paralysed from the chest down. He took up para table tennis in 2021 and, according to the report of his medal, has now won 13 medals in ITTF tournaments, including one gold, four silver and eight bronze.

The pattern across the five results is depth rather than a single standout win. India placed players on the podium across five different classes, in both wheelchair and standing categories, and in both the women's and men's singles. Each semifinal opponent named in the reports was a Paralympic champion or medallist, which sets the level India still has to clear to turn these bronze medals into finals in later tournaments.

For Indian supporters at home and in the diaspora following the Games from abroad, the practical takeaway is that para table tennis is no longer a one-athlete story built around Bhavina Patel. Sahana's and Prachi's first standing-category medals widen the group of Indian paddlers who have proved they can reach a continental podium.

Attention now turns to the rest of India's campaign in Aichi-Nagoya. The five singles bronze medals have already set a new mark for Indian para table tennis at these Games, and any further medals in the remaining events would extend a record that, until this edition, stood at two.
